reason: Multiple independent institutional and reporting sources corroborate the discovery of a candidate second-generation planet orbiting white dwarf HS 0209+0832 based on archival Hubble data.
story: When stars like our Sun run out of fuel, they blow off their outer envelopes and leave behind a dense white dwarf core. Astronomers assumed this was the final chapter for planetary systems. But in a 25-year-old cold case from 1999, the Hubble Space Telescope recorded roughly 100 mystery spectral lines from the white dwarf HS 0209+0832 that scientists could not decipher. Revisiting the data with modern spectral libraries, an international team led by University of Warwick astronomers discovered that the mystery element was niobium, an element forged in the violent death throes of dying stars. Because niobium had never been detected in a white dwarf atmosphere, the researchers realized they were watching a Jupiter-sized world being vaporized. Formed from the shed debris of its parent star's death rather than its birth, this second-generation gas giant orbits just 3.7 million miles out, leaving a comet-like trail of reclaimed ashes falling back onto the dead star.
angle: A dying star can forge heavy elements in its death throes and birth a brand-new, second-generation planet out of its own ashes.

claims.claim: Archival Hubble Space Telescope observations of the white dwarf HS 0209+0832 from 1999 contained around 100 unidentified chemical spectral features.
Reanalysis of the archival Hubble spectra using an updated chemical database revealed that the unexplained lines were caused by the element niobium.
Niobium had never previously been reported in any white dwarf star analyzed before this study.
Elements heavier than iron like niobium do not form through standard thermonuclear fusion in stellar cores, but synthesize during the exotic terminal phases of dying stars.
The study was led by researchers from the University of Warwick and published in the journal Nature Astronomy.
The heavy-element abundance suggests HS 0209+0832 hosts a candidate second-generation planet formed from material cast off during the star's death.
The candidate second-generation planet is estimated to be a gas giant roughly the size of Jupiter.
The planet orbits HS 0209+0832 at a distance of approximately 6 million kilometers (3.7 million miles), much closer than Mercury orbits the Sun.
Archival spectral observations from NASA's retired Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) mission confirmed the strong niobium signatures in the system.
NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) observed the white dwarf for four months and detected periodic brightness variations matching an orbiting planet.
Because the white dwarf is relatively young and hot, its radiation is actively stripping away the nearby planet's atmosphere.
Material stripped from the gas giant likely forms a comet-like tail and a debris disk around the white dwarf, depositing niobium onto the star's surface.
A white dwarf is the dense remnant core of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers into space.
Nicholas Stone, a theoretical astrophysicist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, co-authored the study analyzing the nucleosynthesis of the ejecta.

disputed: Lead author Jamie Williams's pronouns differ across accounts: NASA and ESA releases refer to Williams as 'he', while Universe Today refers to Williams as 'her'. Scripts should avoid gendered pronouns by referring to the researcher by surname.

Universe Today claims the planet could only have formed after its star 'went supernova', whereas the NASA and ESA releases state it was a low-mass star shedding its outer envelope into a planetary nebula/stellar remnant. Scripts should avoid mentioning a supernova and state the star ejected its material during its death throes.
